name: Kotlin/Wasm (JetBrains kotlin-wasm-benchmarks)
workload: are-we-fast-yet style benchmark set (CD, Havlak, JSON, Mandelbrot, nBody, Bounce, List, Permute, Queens, Sieve, Storage, Towers) built once for Kotlin/Wasm and once for Kotlin/JS and run in V8 through kotlinx-benchmark; a second chart runs Compose Multiplatform UI benchmarks (AnimatedVisibility, LazyGrid, VisualEffects) on JVM, Wasm and JS.
claimed_speedup: Relative-time bar chart (Kotlin/JS = 100%, lower is better), values read off the screenshot so approximate (derived from page data): Wasm about 40% on List (roughly 2.5x faster), about 64-80% on CD, Havlak, nBody, Bounce, Permute, Queens, Sieve, Storage and Towers (roughly 1.25-1.6x faster), about 101% on Mandelbrot (no gain), about 173% on JSON (about 1.7x slower). Compose chart (JVM = 100%): Wasm about 155-180% vs JS about 315-400%, so Wasm roughly 2x faster than JS on all three UI benchmarks.
compiler_and_flags: Gradle tasks wasmBenchmark (Kotlin/Wasm), wasmOptBenchmark (Kotlin/Wasm optimised with Binaryen) and jsBenchmark (Kotlin/JS), all in V8; Kotlin version set in gradle.properties; no compiler flags or V8/Node version stated in the README
stars_or_usage: JetBrains/kotlin 53.5k stars; Kotlin/kotlin-wasm-benchmarks 23 stars (last commit 2026-10-07 is for the benchmark repo)
tradeoffs: Needs a WasmGC-capable engine (current Chromium, Firefox, Node); JS interop and DOM access cross the Wasm/JS boundary; Wasm output is larger on first load than hand-tuned JS for small apps (not measured here); string-heavy code is the weak spot (JSON benchmark is slower on Wasm).
caveats: Numbers exist only as two PNG screenshots in the README (read by eye, so +-3 points); the README states no CPU, V8 version, Kotlin version or JIT warm-up settings; the baseline is Kotlin/JS output, not hand-written JS or TypeScript; the README calls the suite work-in-progress; the repo carries three licence badges (Apache-2.0, BSD, MIT) and says to see LICENSE.md, which lists all three for different benchmark sources; the compiler itself (JetBrains/kotlin) is Apache-2.0; JSON benchmark is about 1.7x slower and Mandelbrot is level, so the win is workload-dependent; screenshots may predate the current Kotlin release.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/benchmark?q=wasm listing, then WebAssembly-GC web search (kotlin-wasm-benchmarks)

name: tinymt-wasm-typescript-benchmark (minimal AssemblyScript TinyMT32)
baseline: TypeScript TinyMT32 running in V8 (Node 24.18.0) and C++ TinyMT32 compiled with Emscripten and embind
workload: TinyMT 32-bit pseudo random generator producing 10 to 10,000 integers or floats per call, four implementations (minimal AssemblyScript, AssemblyScript with arrays, C++ via Emscripten, TypeScript), run with vitest bench on Node 24.18.0; also output size.
claimed_speedup: Ints x10: AssemblyScript 15,295,751 hz vs C++/Emscripten 14,218,306 vs TypeScript 12,235,627 (1.25x TypeScript, 1.08x C++, derived from page data). Ints x10,000: 21,602 vs 19,316 vs 15,175 hz (1.42x TypeScript, 1.12x C++, derived). Floats x10,000: AssemblyScript 20,544 hz vs C++ 17,688 vs TypeScript 235 hz (about 87x TypeScript, per the README). Size: minimal AssemblyScript 1,260 bytes (wasm plus JS glue) vs C++ 36,445 vs TypeScript 3,568.
compiler_and_flags: asc 0.28.20 with --optimizeLevel 3 --shrinkLevel 2 --enable simd --enable stringref --enable relaxed-simd --noAssert --converge, then wasm-opt -O3; C++ with em++ -O3 -Oz -lembind -std=c++20 (the later -Oz overrides -O3, so the C++ build is size-optimised); Node 24.18.0, TypeScript 6.0
tradeoffs: Fastest build uses only i32/u32 locals (the 128-bit state is unrolled into four variables, no arrays or strings); the same AssemblyScript with Array or StaticArray is 4-5x slower than TypeScript (2.7M hz vs 12.2M hz for ints x10) and 3.5-6x larger, so the win needs hand-restricted code. Native C++ is 2-4x faster than every Wasm build.
caveats: Single-author benchmark repo with no stated CPU or OS; no licence file, so code is reference only; float comparison is inflated because the TypeScript version allocates an ArrayBuffer, Uint8Array and DataView per float (author says so), where Wasm has a single reinterpret instruction; C++ baseline compiled effectively with -Oz and called through embind; integer comparison is the fairer one (1.1-1.4x). Evidence for AssemblyScript (already catalogued) rather than a library of its own.
found_via: GitHub: web search 'AssemblyScript vs JavaScript benchmark github repository results' (result list)

name: LeanyLabs assemblyscript-benchmarks (factorial)
baseline: JavaScript (recursive factorial) in V8 under Node
workload: Six micro-benchmarks run with benchmark.js: add (boundary crossing), factorial(20), squareArray, calcSinLookup, importCallback and averageIfLess over 2 million float64 values.
claimed_speedup: factorial: AssemblyScript 14,076,129 ops/sec vs JavaScript 6,483,418 ops/sec (2.17x, derived from page data). calcSinLookup tied (11,450 vs 11,417 ops/sec). JavaScript wins the other four: add 697M vs 126M, squareArray 822k vs 432k, importCallback 352k vs 24k, averageIfLess 338 vs 294 ops/sec.
compiler_and_flags: asc (assemblyscript ^0.18.4) release target in asconfig.json: optimizeLevel 3, shrinkLevel 0, converge, noAssert; benchmark.js 2.1.4; Node version not stated
hardware: Intel Core i5-8250 (as written in the README), 16 GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04 LTS
tradeoffs: AssemblyScript pays for every JS/Wasm boundary crossing: passing arrays and calling imports is 2-15x slower than plain JavaScript, so only compute-heavy code with small arguments wins.
caveats: Mixed result: AssemblyScript wins one of six workloads, ties one and loses four, so this is evidence of a narrow win (and of boundary cost), not a general speedup; 2021 numbers on AssemblyScript 0.18 and an unnamed Node version; the recursive factorial(20) is a tiny kernel and the two sides do not compute the same thing: the AssemblyScript version is i32 (assembly/index.ts: factorial(i: i32): i32), so 20! wraps around, while the JavaScript version returns the exact float64 value; the harness does not check results.
found_via: GitHub: web search 'AssemblyScript vs JavaScript benchmark github repository results' (result list)

name: wasm-and-ffi-performance-comparison-in-node (Rust WASM Collatz)
baseline: JavaScript Number-based Collatz loop in Node (V8), and a Rust native addon via FFI
workload: Collatz step count for input 670617279 in Node, benchmark.js, comparing a JS function, a Rust FFI addon and Rust compiled with wasm-pack.
claimed_speedup: JS 32,172 ops/sec, FFI 225,918 ops/sec, WASM 1,465,898 ops/sec; WASM is 45.6x JS and 6.5x FFI (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: wasm-pack build --target nodejs --release; Cargo release profile lto = true; wasm-bindgen 0.2.92; Node version not stated
tradeoffs: Needs a Rust toolchain and wasm-pack; each call crosses the JS/Wasm boundary with a u64 (BigInt) argument; result only holds for a tight integer loop.
caveats: Single-commit toy benchmark; no CPU or Node version stated; the Collatz sequence for 670617279 takes 986 steps and peaks near 9.7e11 (computed while checking), above the int32 range, so the JS version runs float64 % and / while the Rust version uses u64 integer ops, which probably explains much of the 45x gap; a hand-tuned JS version (or a fairer integer kernel) would likely be much closer; the wasm wrapper converts the Number argument to BigInt on every call; README gives speculative reasons for the win without profiling.

name: utf-as
baseline: AssemblyScript standard library String.UTF8.decode / String.UTF8.encode (running as Wasm in V8)
workload: UTF-8 to UTF-16 decode and UTF-16 to UTF-8 encode over 15 payloads (14 HTML pages in different languages plus an emoji text file from the simdutf fixture set), SIMD kernels ported from simdutf's Westmere SSE4 code to 128-bit Wasm SIMD, plus UTF-8 and UTF-16 validators.
claimed_speedup: README: UTF8.decode 2.1-6.7x faster than String.UTF8.decode, UTF8.encode 4.3-9.4x faster than String.UTF8.encode on the HTML payloads; UTF8.validate up to 55.4 GB/s (no stdlib equivalent). Chart values read from the PNGs (approximate, v8): english.html decode about 17.5 GB/s vs 2.5 GB/s stdlib (7.0x, derived from page data), encode about 11.5 vs 1.2 GB/s; most other pages decode 4-11 GB/s vs 1.8-2.3 GB/s and encode 4-9 GB/s vs 0.9-1.1 GB/s; emoji.txt decode 1.6 GB/s (SIMD) vs 2.5 GB/s stdlib, encode 1.0 vs 1.0.
compiler_and_flags: asc with --enable simd for the quoted figures (SWAR fallback otherwise); runs in V8 (chart file names end in -v8); npm run bench:vs-stdlib reproduces; asc version not stated in the README
tradeoffs: AssemblyScript only; SIMD build needs Wasm SIMD support (SWAR default path works without it but is 1.5-4x faster rather than 2-9x); pointer-based Unsafe APIs and scratch buffers, one-shot functions are not reentrant.
caveats: Baseline is the AssemblyScript stdlib, not JavaScript or C++; CPU and asc version are not stated anywhere I could find; numbers live in PNG charts and the README summary (README range 2.1-6.7x decode, while the chart bar for english.html reads about 7x, so the README range may be from another run); emoji (4-byte) input is no faster or slower than the stdlib; single-author young repo.
found_via: npm registry search keywords:assemblyscript (utf-as), then the GitHub README and benchmark chart PNGs

name: as-str
baseline: AssemblyScript standard library String methods (native String ops compiled by asc, run in V8 15.1.42)
workload: Per-operation microbenchmarks (slice, trim, indexOf, includes, split, toUpperCase, replace and others) of zero-copy string views with SWAR and SIMD scanning versus the same String method; 2 kb input for the throughput chart; benchmark run via as-bench.
claimed_speedup: Per-operation chart for v0.2.2 (native = 1.0x, str built with SIMD; bar labels, read from the PNG): replace 11x, indexOf 8.2x, includes 8.1x, toUpperCase 3.9x, toLowerCase 3.8x, replaceAll 3.5x, lastIndexOf 2.5x, trim/trimStart/trimEnd 1.4-1.5x, padStart 1.4x; slower on startsWith 0.7x, endsWith 0.8x, length 0.8x; slice, substring, split, equals, repeat, concat about 1.0x. Throughput chart (2 kb input): indexOf about 1 vs 6 Mops/s, toUpperCase about 1 vs 5 Mops/s.
compiler_and_flags: asc with --enable simd for the SIMD tier (SWAR tier is the default without it); V8 15.1.42 per the chart footer; other flags not stated
tradeoffs: A str is a 3-field view over a UTF-16 string, so it is a different type from String (conversions needed at API boundaries); several operations (startsWith, endsWith, length, charAt) are slower than native; semantics mirror AssemblyScript String, not JavaScript.
caveats: Charts are from release v0.2.2 while the repo is now at v0.6.0; no CPU or OS stated; baseline is the AssemblyScript stdlib, not JavaScript or C++; values are read from chart images (the bar labels are rounded); the micro-benchmarks use short inputs and equal-sized needles chosen by the author.
found_via: npm registry search keywords:assemblyscript, then github.com/JairusSW repositories page and the repo's chart PNGs

name: JavaScript-vs-WebAssembly-Comparative-Analysis (Rust wasm matrix multiply)
baseline: JavaScript matrix multiplication in V8 (Chromium; Firefox also run)
workload: n x n matrix multiplication (64 to 512) and a particle-physics rendering demo, written in parallel in JavaScript and Rust (wasm-pack, wasm-bindgen, web target), automated with Playwright.
claimed_speedup: Matrix multiply, JS vs WASM in ms: 64x64 0.50 vs 0.50 (1.00x), 128x128 3.45 vs 2.20 (1.57x), 256x256 28.85 vs 15.65 (1.84x), 512x512 218.05 vs 136.10 (1.60x). Particle physics step 1.7-2.8x faster in WASM but frame rate equal (about 60 FPS, GPU bound). P95 latency 28-31% worse in WASM at n>=256.
compiler_and_flags: Rust stable with wasm-pack >= 0.13 and wasm-bindgen, --target web; opt-level and wasm-opt settings not stated
tradeoffs: Needs a Rust toolchain and wasm-pack build step; large-matrix tail latency was worse in WASM (cache pressure per the author); GPU-bound workloads show no gain.
caveats: Academic single-commit repo; no licence (README says code is for academic and educational purposes), so reference only; CPU, OS and browser versions are not given in the README (docs/ENV.md linked but not read); the repo is both the code and the report, no independent reproduction; speedup is modest (1.5-1.8x) and only on a naive O(n^3) kernel.
found_via: GitHub: web search 'Zig compiled to WebAssembly npm library benchmark faster than JavaScript' (result list)
